title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
oneLineScope: How a token gathers information from other tokens via weighted soft lookup — the core operation of the transformer.
prose:
Every position in a sequence needs to look at the others. A pronoun needs its antecedent; a verb needs its subject; a word with several senses needs the neighbors that disambiguate it. The recurrent models in the RNN/LSTM baseline carried that context forward one step at a time, squeezing an entire left-hand history through a single fixed-width state vector — a bottleneck that grew tighter the longer the sequence got. Attention discards the bottleneck and the sequentiality at once: it lets each position reach directly across the whole sequence and pull in a content-dependent mixture of what it finds, in one parallel operation rather than \(n\) sequential ones. This node is the mechanism that does the pulling.

A soft, differentiable lookup

The cleanest way to think about attention is as a soft dictionary lookup. An ordinary lookup — a hash map, a database index — matches a query against stored keys and returns the one value whose key matches exactly. That is a hard, discrete operation: it has no useful derivative, so it cannot sit inside a network you want to train by gradient descent. Attention is its continuous relaxation. Instead of demanding an exact match and returning one value, it scores the query against every key, turns those scores into a probability distribution, and returns the weighted average of all the values. Nothing is selected and nothing is discarded; everything is blended, each value weighted by how well its key matched the query. In the limit of one sharply dominant match the blend approaches a hard lookup, but the operation stays smooth and differentiable everywhere, which is exactly what lets the projections that produce the queries and keys be learned.

If you know the statistical alignment models from machine translation — the IBM models, or HMM-based alignment — you already know the shape of this idea. There, a latent alignment variable decides which source word a target word is generated from, and EM gives you a soft posterior over alignments. Attention is that same move made differentiable and learned end to end: the alignment weights are computed on the fly from the representations themselves, not estimated as a separate latent-variable model, and gradients flow straight through them into the rest of the network. The alignment-and-attention node traces that lineage in detail; here we take the operation as Vaswani et al. published it and pin down its mechanics.

Queries, keys, and values

Each position emits three vectors, all linear projections of its current representation:

  • a query — “what am I looking for?”
  • a key — “what do I offer to others?”
  • a value — “what do I actually contribute if attended to?”

Separating the key from the value is the quietly important design choice. The key governs whether a position is attended to; the value governs what is delivered when it is. A token can advertise itself one way and carry a payload of a different character, and the two roles are trained independently. The projections are linear and learned, which is what lets the same token play different roles in different contexts: the network discovers, through the loss, which directions of the representation space should drive matching (the key/query subspace) and which should be passed along as content (the value subspace). Note that nothing forces \(d_k\) and \(d_v\) to be equal — they are independent hyperparameters, and only the value dimension flows out to the next layer.

The equation, with dimensions

Let the input be \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\), one row per position (\(n\) positions, width \(d_{\text{model}}\)). Three learned weight matrices project it:

\[ Q = X W_Q,\quad K = X W_K,\quad V = X W_V \]

with \(W_Q, W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}\) and \(W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}\), giving \(Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}\) and \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}\). The operation itself is one line:

\[ \operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) V \]

Read it left to right by shape. \(Q K^{\top}\) is \(n \times n\): entry \((i, j)\) is the dot product of query \(i\) with key \(j\) — a raw compatibility score, every position against every position. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) rescales those scores (see below). The \(\operatorname{softmax}\) is applied row-wise, so each row becomes a probability distribution that sums to one: row \(i\) is the set of weights position \(i\) places on every position's value. Call that stochastic matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\). Finally \(A V\) is \(n \times d_v\): each output row is the weighted average of all value vectors, weighted by that row's attention distribution. One position in, one mixed-context vector out — for all \(n\) positions in a single pair of matrix multiplies.

It helps to put numbers to the shapes once. Take a toy sequence of \(n = 10\) tokens with \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\) and \(d_k = d_v = 64\). Then \(Q, K, V\) are each \(10 \times 64\); the score matrix \(Q K^{\top}\) is \(10 \times 10\) (one hundred query–key comparisons); after scaling and the row-wise softmax, \(A\) is still \(10 \times 10\) with each of its ten rows summing to one; and \(A V\) is \(10 \times 64\) — ten context vectors, one per position, each a convex combination of the ten value vectors. The \(n \times n\) score matrix is the object to keep your eye on: it is where “who looks at whom” lives, and every later variation on attention is, at bottom, a different way of shaping it.

Why divide by √d_k

This is the one detail people skip and then misremember, so it is worth stating carefully. Take query and key entries to be roughly independent with zero mean and unit variance; their dot product over \(d_k\) dimensions then has variance on the order of \(d_k\), so its typical magnitude grows like \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Feed scores of that scale into a softmax and it saturates: almost all the mass collapses onto the single largest score, the distribution becomes nearly one-hot, and the gradient through the softmax goes flat — exactly the vanishing-gradient regime you want to avoid, and worse at larger \(d_k\) precisely where you would hope for more capacity. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalizes the score variance back to order one, keeping the softmax in its responsive range regardless of head size. It is a variance-control trick, not a probabilistic identity; the full argument is the footnote in §3.2.1 of Vaswani et al.

Masking

Attention as written lets every position see every other, which is correct for an encoder reading a complete input at once. Two situations require suppressing specific entries, and both do it the same way — by setting scores to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, so the exponential sends them to exactly zero weight. The first is the causal mask: for autoregressive generation, predicting token \(t\) from tokens \(1{\ldots}t{-}1\), a position must not peek at its own future, so every score \((i, j)\) with \(j > i\) is masked out. The property then holds for all rows in parallel without changing the equation's shape; this is the hinge the autoregressive-lm node turns on. The second is the padding mask: when sequences of different lengths are batched together and padded to a common length, the padding positions are masked so no real token attends to filler. Same mechanism, different bookkeeping.

What it costs, and where it goes next

The score matrix is \(n \times n\), so both compute and memory scale as \(O(n^2 d)\) in the sequence length. For the modest \(n\) of this era that is cheap, and — crucially — it is parallel: every query–key score is independent, so the whole operation is two big matrix multiplies a GPU can do at once, with a constant number of sequential steps rather than the \(n\) steps an RNN must take. That short, fixed path between any two positions is the property that finally made long-range dependencies learnable. (The same quadratic term is what later long-context work spends its effort attacking, but that is a frontier-era concern, out of scope here.) With the single-head operation in hand, two directions open immediately: running several of these in parallel on different projected subspaces (multi-head attention), and confronting the fact that, since attention is a sum over an unordered set, nothing here knows the order of the tokens at all — the problem positional encoding exists to solve.

diagrams.altText: A left-to-right pipeline. Input matrix X (n by d_model) projects via W_Q, W_K, W_V into Q (n by d_k), K (n by d_k), and V (n by d_v). Q and K feed a matrix multiply producing the score matrix Q-K-transpose (n by n), which is divided by the square root of d_k and passed through a row-wise softmax to give the attention weight matrix A (n by n). A and V feed a final matrix multiply producing the output (n by d_v). A note marks that a causal mask sets above-diagonal scores to minus infinity before the softmax.

diagrams.caption: The soft-lookup intuition: a query blends all values in proportion to how well it matches each key.
diagrams.altText: A single query card on the left reading 'what am I looking for?' connects to a row of several key cards each reading 'what I offer', and behind each key sits a value card. Bands of varying thickness run from the query to each key, suggesting a soft weighted match across all of them rather than selecting one. The result on the right is shown as a blend of the values weighted by match strength.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual analogy illustration of attention as a 'soft lookup'. On the left, a single query drawn as a small labeled card reading 'what am I looking for?'. In the middle, a row of several key cards each reading 'what I offer', and behind or beside each key card a matching value card carrying a small payload. Draw bands of varying thickness from the single query to each key, the thicker bands meaning a stronger match; emphasize that the query connects to ALL keys at once with different strengths rather than picking exactly one. On the right, show the result as a blended value — a mixture of the value cards combined in proportion to the match strengths. No equations and no tensor shapes; this is the plain-language intuition companion to the structural diagram. Conceptual analogy: vibe over precise labels.

expansion: Deeper treatment the prose deliberately omits, to be expanded strictly from the cited sources: (1) the full variance argument for √d_k scaling, including the independence/unit-variance assumptions and what breaks when they fail; (2) the comparison to additive (Bahdanau) attention and why the dot-product form wins on speed despite similar quality at small d_k — Vaswani §3.2.1; (3) complexity analysis O(n²·d) in time and memory, and the path-length / parallelism argument from §4 that motivates attention over recurrence; (4) the precise softmax-gradient saturation analysis.
